Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Current Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) frameworks are predominantly text-centric, necessitating a preprocessing stage that converts multi-modal documents (such as PDFs, textbooks, and manuals) into plain text. This conversion typically relies on Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and layout analysis, which inevitably introduces cascading errors and strips away critical visual information. By decoupling text from its spatial layout and discarding figures, charts, and diagrams, traditional RAG systems create an information bottleneck, rendering them incapable of answering queries that depend on visual context or complex document formatting.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can eliminate the destructive text-parsing stage entirely by treating document pages as images throughout the entire RAG pipeline. By utilizing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for both the retrieval and generation phases, we aim to preserve the document's information in its original visual format. We believe that encoding the "raw" pixels of a page will allow the system to retain and reason over visual cues (layout, typography, and graphics) that are currently lost in text-based approaches, thereby streamlining the architecture and improving accuracy on multi-modal tasks.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose "VisRAG," a dual-stage pipeline designed to operate directly on visual inputs.

**1. Vision-Based Retrieval (VisRAG-Ret)**
We will design a dual-encoder architecture akin to dense passage retrieval, but adapted for multi-modality:
*   **Query Encoding:** A VLM component will process the user's textual query.
*   **Document Encoding:** Instead of processing extracted text, the VLM will process the rasterized image of the document page.
*   **Embedding Strategy:** To derive a fixed-size vector representation from the VLM's output, we will employ a pooling mechanism on the final hidden states. This will compress the visual and semantic features of the page into a dense embedding optimized for similarity search.
*   **Optimization:** The encoders will be trained using contrastive loss functions to maximize the similarity between a query and its corresponding visual document page while minimizing similarity to negative samples.

**2. Vision-Based Generation (VisRAG-Gen)**
Upon retrieving the top candidate pages (images), we will feed them directly into a generative VLM alongside the text query to produce an answer. We will explore mechanisms to handle multiple retrieved images, including:
*   **Page Concatenation:** Stitching multiple retrieved page images into a single composite image to allow the VLM to reason across different contexts simultaneously.
*   **Weighted Selection:** Generating answers from individual pages and aggregating the results based on the model's confidence scores to select the most probable response.
*   **Multi-Image Input:** Utilizing VLMs capable of accepting sequences of images natively to perform cross-page reasoning.

## Expected Contribution
This project aims to establish a new standard for RAG pipelines by proving the feasibility of a "pure-vision" approach. Theoretically, this simplifies the RAG stack by removing the dependency on external OCR and layout parsing tools. Practically, this method is expected to significantly enhance performance on real-world documents where information is distributed across text and visual elements, ensuring that the model utilizes the full richness of the original data without intermediate loss.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

### Data Construction
We constructed datasets combining Visual Question Answering (VQA) benchmarks and synthetic data.
*   **VQA Datasets (Evaluation & Training):**
    *   **ArXivQA:** Arxiv Figures.
    *   **ChartQA:** Charts.
    *   **MP-DocVQA:** Industrial Documents (Validation split used for evaluation).
    *   **InfoVQA:** Infographics (Validation split used for evaluation).
    *   **PlotQA:** Scientific Plots.
    *   **SlideVQA:** Slide Decks (Contains multi-hop questions).
    *   *Note:* Context-dependent queries were filtered out using a GPT-4o classification step.
*   **Synthetic Data (Training only):**
    *   We collected open-source PDFs (Textbooks, ICML/NeurIPS papers, Manuals) and generated query-document pairs using GPT-4o.
*   **Corpus:** The retrieval corpus consisted of documents associated with each query from the training and evaluation sets.

### Evaluation Metrics
*   **Retrieval:** Mean Reciprocal Rank at 10 (MRR@10) and Recall at 10 (Recall@10).
*   **Generation:** Answer Accuracy (Exact Match). A relaxed exact match was used for numeric responses allowing a 5% error margin.

### Model Architectures
*   **VisRAG-Ret (Retriever):**
    *   **Architecture:** Dual-encoder based on MiniCPM-V 2.0.
    *   **Components:** SigLIP vision encoder + MiniCPM language model.
    *   **Pooling:** Position-weighted mean pooling over the last-layer hidden states.
    *   **Loss Function:** InfoNCE loss.
*   **VisRAG-Gen (Generator):**
    *   **Single-Image VLM:** MiniCPM-V 2.0. Methods tested: Page Concatenation and Weighted Selection.
    *   **Multi-Image VLM:** MiniCPM-V 2.6 and GPT-4o (accepting multiple images directly).

### Baselines and Comparisons
*   **Document Parsing (Text Extraction):**
    *   **Pytesseract:** Python wrapper for Tesseract OCR.
    *   **PPOCR:** PaddlePaddle OCR with "Adjacent Merging" (merging nearby boxes) and "Layout Preserving" (inserting spaces/line breaks) strategies.
    *   **Captioner:** Model-based parsing using MiniCPM-V 2.0 fine-tuned on (document image, text) pairs.
*   **Retrievers:**
    *   **Text-based:** BM25, bge-large-en-v1.5, NV-Embed-v2, MiniCPM (text-only embedding).
    *   **Vision-based:** SigLIP, ColPali (page embedding model).
*   **Generators:**
    *   **Text-based:** MiniCPM (OCR), GPT-4o (OCR).

### Implementation Details
*   **Hardware:** 8 NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs.
*   **Retriever Training:** Fine-tuned using in-batch negatives for 1 epoch.
*   **Batch Size:** 128.
*   **Temperature:** 0.02 (for InfoNCE).
*   **Generator Inference:** No fine-tuning; off-the-shelf models were used.
*   **Parsing Model Training:** MiniCPM-V 2.0 captioner trained with batch size 2048, learning rate 5e-6, for 1 epoch.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Observation 1 (Overall Performance):** In end-to-end generation accuracy, VisRAG consistently outperformed TextRAG across all datasets. Using MiniCPM-V 2.6 as the generator, VisRAG achieved approximately 53% accuracy compared to TextRAG's 37% (a ~40% relative improvement). With GPT-4o, VisRAG achieved roughly 52% accuracy versus TextRAG's 43% (a ~20% relative improvement).
*   **Observation 2 (Pipeline Breakdown):** Analysis of the InfographicsVQA dataset showed that VisRAG achieved a higher rate of correct document retrieval compared to TextRAG (79.4% vs 76.9%). More significantly, given a correctly retrieved document, VisRAG demonstrated a much higher success rate in generating the correct answer (51.1% vs 24.8% final correct generation rate).
*   **Observation 3 (Data Efficiency):** In terms of training data efficiency, VisRAG-Ret required significantly fewer training examples to match the performance of text-based baselines. VisRAG-Ret matched the performance of bge-large (OCR) with approximately 20K examples, whereas MiniCPM (OCR) required about 75K examples.
*   **Observation 4 (Generalization):** VisRAG-Ret maintained a performance advantage (approx. 13%) over MiniCPM (OCR) even as the number of training examples increased to 240K.
*   **Observation 5 (Document Type Sensitivity):** The performance gap between VisRAG and TextRAG (and VisRAG-SigLIP) was sensitive to document length. VisRAG's relative advantage over TextRAG increased as the length of the positive document (number of text tokens) decreased, suggesting visual encoders are superior for documents with sparse text or high visual density.
*   **Observation 6 (Modality Fusion):** Fusing text and visual embeddings (MiniCPM (OCR) + SigLIP via RRF) improved performance over individual baselines but still underperformed the unified VisRAG-Ret model (e.g., Average In-domain MRR@10 of 76.87 for Fusion vs 77.91 for VisRAG-Ret).
*   **Observation 7 (Multi-Page Reasoning):** Single-image VLMs (MiniCPM-V 2.0) using Page Concatenation or Weighted Selection did not show performance improvements when increasing retrieved documents from top-1 to top-3. In contrast, multi-image capable VLMs (MiniCPM-V 2.6 and GPT-4o) showed performance gains as more documents were retrieved.
*   **Observation 8 (Qualitative Failure of TextRAG):** Case studies revealed that TextRAG failures were often due to OCR inability to handle decorative fonts or the loss of spatial layout information (e.g., confusing labels in charts/infographics), which VisRAG handled correctly by preserving the original visual format.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Current Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems are predominantly text-centric. When dealing with real-world multi-modal documents—such as textbooks, manuals, and financial reports containing interleaving text, figures, charts, and complex layouts—these systems rely on a "parsing-first" approach. This involves a cascade of Optical Character Recognition (OCR), layout analysis, and text extraction to convert documents into plain text segments before retrieval or generation can occur.

This parsing stage creates a critical bottleneck. First, it inevitably introduces errors (e.g., OCR misrecognizing characters). Second, and more importantly, it causes severe information loss; visual cues, spatial relationships, and non-textual elements (charts, diagrams) are often discarded or poorly transcribed. Consequently, the downstream Large Language Model (LLM) loses access to the rich context inherent in the original document format, limiting its reasoning capabilities on complex, visually-rich data.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose **VisRAG** (Vision-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a pipeline that eliminates the text parsing stage entirely. We hypothesize that by treating document pages as images throughout the entire RAG process, we can maximize information retention.

Our core premise is that a Vision-Language Model (VLM) can serve as both the retriever and the generator. By embedding the visual representation of a document page directly, we can perform retrieval in a multi-modal embedding space. Subsequently, by feeding the retrieved raw document images directly into a VLM generator, we enable the model to reason over the original visual data (text, layout, and figures) without the degradation caused by intermediate text conversion.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct a dual-stage framework consisting of **VisRAG-Ret** (Retrieval) and **VisRAG-Gen** (Generation).

### 1. VisRAG-Ret: VLM-Based Retrieval

We will design a bi-encoder architecture where the query is processed as text and the document is processed as an image. We will utilize a VLM composed of a vision encoder (e.g., SigLIP) and a language model (e.g., MiniCPM).

**Embedding Extraction Strategy:**
Unlike standard text retrievers that use `[CLS]` tokens, generative VLMs utilize causal attention. To derive a robust vector representation from the sequence of hidden states produced by the VLM, we will implement **position-weighted mean pooling** over the last-layer hidden states. This assigns higher importance to later tokens in the sequence, which aggregates information more effectively in causal architectures.

Formally, given a sequence of hidden states, the embedding $\mathbf{v}$ is calculated as:
$$ \mathbf { v } = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { S } w _ { i } \mathbf { h } _ { i } $$
where:
*   $\mathbf{h}_i$ is the $i$-th hidden state of the VLM's last layer.
*   $S$ is the sequence length.
*   $w_i$ is the weight for the $i$-th token, defined as:
    $$ w _ { i } = \frac { i } { \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { S } j } $$

**Optimization Objective:**
We will optimize the retriever using the InfoNCE loss function to maximize the similarity between the query and the positive document image while minimizing similarity with negative samples. The loss is defined as:
$$ l ( q , d ^ { + } , D ^ { - } ) = - \log \frac { \exp ( s ( q , d ^ { + } ) / \tau ) } { \exp ( s ( q , d ^ { + } ) / \tau ) + \sum _ { d ^ { - } \in D ^ { - } } \exp ( s ( q , d ^ { - } ) / \tau ) } $$
where:
*   $q$ is the query embedding.
*   $d^+$ is the embedding of the positive document image.
*   $D^-$ is the set of negative document images.
*   $s(q, d)$ denotes the cosine similarity between the query and document embeddings.
*   $\tau$ is the temperature hyperparameter.

### 2. VisRAG-Gen: VLM-Based Generation

Once the top-$k$ document images are retrieved (denoted as set $\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{R}}$), we must feed them into a generative VLM to produce an answer $a$. We will implement three distinct strategies to handle multi-document contexts, accommodating different VLM architectures.

**Strategy A: Page Concatenation (For Single-Image VLMs)**
For VLMs restricted to single-image inputs, we will stitch the retrieved document images into a single large image canvas. We will utilize horizontal concatenation:
$$ a \gets \mathrm { V L M - S i n g l e } ( q , \mathrm { C o n c a t } ( \{ d | d \in \mathcal { D } _ { \mathcal { R } } \} ) ) $$
where $\mathrm{Concat}$ represents the image concatenation operation.

**Strategy B: Weighted Selection (For Single-Image VLMs)**
To avoid resolution loss from concatenation, we will process each retrieved page individually and aggregate the results. We will generate a candidate answer for every page and select the final answer based on a confidence score that combines generation probability and retrieval similarity.

The final confidence is defined as:
$$ P ( a | q , \mathcal { D } _ { \mathcal { R } } ) = P ( a | q , d ) \cdot \lambda ( q , d ) $$
where:
*   $P(a|q, d)$ is the generation probability (reciprocal of perplexity) of answer $a$ given document $d$.
*   $\lambda(q, d)$ is the normalized retrieval score, calculated via softmax:
    $$ \lambda ( q , d ) = \frac { e ^ { s ( q , d ) } } { \sum _ { d ^ { \prime } \in \mathcal { D } _ { \mathcal { R } } } e ^ { s ( q , d ^ { \prime } ) } } $$

**Strategy C: Native Multi-Image Processing**
For advanced VLMs that support multi-image inputs inherently (e.g., MiniCPM-V 2.6), we will feed the discrete set of images directly to perform cross-image reasoning:
$$ a \gets \mathsf { V L M \mathrm { - M u l t i } } ( q , \{ d | d \in \mathcal { D } _ { \mathcal { R } } \} ) $$

### 3. Data Construction Pipeline

To train the VisRAG-Ret module, we require high-quality query-document pairs where the document is an image.

1.  **Source Aggregation:** We will aggregate varied Visual Question Answering (VQA) datasets (e.g., ArXivQA, ChartQA, DocVQA) covering diverse domains like industrial documents, scientific plots, and slides.
2.  **Synthetic Data Generation:** We will augment this with open-source PDFs. We will employ a powerful VLM (e.g., GPT-4o) to generate synthetic queries based on specific pages from these PDFs.
3.  **Query Filtering:** To ensure retrieval relevance, we must remove context-dependent queries (e.g., "What is the title of *this* page?"). We will implement a filtering stage using an LLM prompted to classify and discard queries that lack specific entity references or are ambiguous without immediate context.

## Expected Contribution

This research expects to establish a new paradigm for RAG systems dealing with visually rich documents. By theoretically and empirically validating that **pixels** can serve as the fundamental unit of retrieval and generation, we aim to:
1.  Eliminate the engineering complexity and error propagation of OCR/parsing pipelines.
2.  Demonstrate that weighted mean pooling on VLM hidden states allows for effective dense retrieval in visual space.
3.  Prove that preserving original visual layout significantly enhances generation accuracy for multi-modal queries compared to text-only baselines.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). Upstream's own Semantic Scholar client goes through the shield.
notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
